title: Nature's Treasures
description: Grade 6 Science: Earth's natural resources (air, water, soil, minerals), renewable and non-renewable resources, and how to use them sustainably. Notes and a test.

topics.title: Earth's Natural Resources
topics.concept:
Everything we use comes, in the end, from nature. The useful materials we obtain from the Earth are called natural resources. Air, water, soil, sunlight, minerals, forests and fuels are all natural resources — nature’s treasures that make life possible.

  • Air — a mixture of gases. We need its oxygen to breathe; plants need its carbon dioxide to make food. Moving air (wind) is also used to make electricity.
  • Water — needed by every living thing for drinking, growing crops and countless daily uses. Most of Earth’s water is in the salty oceans; only a little is usable fresh water.
  • Soil — the loose top layer of the Earth in which plants grow. It holds water and nutrients, and is home to many small creatures. Soil takes a very long time to form.
  • Minerals — useful substances dug out from rocks inside the Earth, such as iron, copper, gold, coal and salt. We use them to make metals, tools, machines and more.

Resources are of two kinds. Renewable resources can be replaced by nature in a fairly short time or do not run out — sunlight, wind, water and forests (if cared for). Non-renewable resources took millions of years to form and will run out if used up — coal, petroleum (oil) and natural gas, together called fossil fuels, and most minerals.

examples.problem: Example 1: Sort these as renewable or non-renewable: sunlight, coal, wind, petroleum.
examples.solution:
Renewable resources do not run out; non-renewable ones do.

  • Renewable: sunlight, wind.
  • Non-renewable: coal, petroleum.
examples.answer: Renewable: sunlight and wind. Non-renewable: coal and petroleum.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are coal, petroleum and natural gas called fossil fuels, and why must we use them carefully?
examples.solution:
Fossil fuels formed long ago and cannot be quickly replaced.

  • They formed from the remains of plants and animals buried for millions of years.
  • They are non-renewable, so they will run out if wasted.
examples.answer: They formed from once-living things over millions of years; being non-renewable, they will run out, so we must use them carefully.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name two natural resources we get from the air.
examples.solution:
Think about what air provides.

  • Oxygen for breathing.
  • Wind (moving air), used to make electricity.
examples.answer: Oxygen (to breathe) and wind (to generate electricity).

recap:
• Natural resources are useful materials from nature: air, water, soil, minerals, forests, fuels.
  • Renewable resources do not run out or are quickly replaced (sunlight, wind, water, forests).
  • Non-renewable resources took millions of years to form and can run out (coal, petroleum, gas — the fossil fuels, and most minerals).
  • Soil and minerals come from the Earth; air gives oxygen and wind.

quiz.q: Useful materials we obtain from nature are called:
quiz.explanation: Useful materials obtained from nature are natural resources.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-renewable resource?
quiz.explanation: Coal is a fossil fuel that took millions of years to form and will run out.

topics.title: Sustainability and Resource Preservation
topics.concept:
Natural resources are limited, and many of them — especially fossil fuels and minerals — cannot be replaced once used up. If we waste them or use them faster than nature can replace them, future generations will be left with too little. Using resources wisely and carefully, so that enough is left for the future, is called sustainability (or sustainable use).

A simple and powerful guide is the rule of the three R’s:

  • Reduce — use less; do not waste. Switch off lights and fans when not needed; close taps; use only what you need.
  • Reuse — use things again instead of throwing them away. Carry a cloth bag, use both sides of paper, refill bottles.
  • Recycle — send used materials like paper, glass, metal and plastic to be made into new things, so fewer fresh resources are used.

We can also help by choosing renewable energy — using the Sun (solar energy) and the wind, which never run out and do not pollute, instead of burning fossil fuels. Planting trees (afforestation) protects soil, gives oxygen and supports wildlife, while saving water and electricity conserves precious resources. Protecting our air, water, soil and forests from pollution keeps these treasures useful for everyone. Caring for nature’s resources today is the way to make sure they last for tomorrow.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is sustainability (sustainable use of resources)?
examples.solution:
It is about balancing today’s needs with the future.

  • Using resources wisely and carefully.
  • So that enough is left for future generations.
examples.answer: Sustainability is using natural resources wisely and carefully so that enough is left for the future.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the three R’s and give one example of each.
examples.solution:
Recall the waste-cutting rule.

  • Reduce — switch off unused lights.
  • Reuse — carry a cloth bag again and again.
  • Recycle — send paper to be made into new paper.
examples.answer: Reduce (switch off unused lights), Reuse (use a cloth bag again), Recycle (send paper to be made into new paper).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is using solar and wind energy better than burning coal?
examples.solution:
Compare renewable and non-renewable sources.

  • Sun and wind are renewable — they never run out.
  • They do not pollute, unlike burning coal.
examples.answer: Because the Sun and wind are renewable and do not pollute, while coal is non-renewable and causes pollution.

recap:
• Sustainability = using resources wisely so enough is left for the future.
  • Follow the three R’s: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.
  • Prefer renewable energy (solar, wind); plant trees; save water and electricity.
  • Protect air, water, soil and forests from pollution so resources last.

quiz.q: Using natural resources wisely so that enough is left for the future is called:
quiz.explanation: Sustainable (wise) use that protects the future is sustainability.

quiz.q: Sending used paper, glass and metal to be made into new things is called:
quiz.explanation: Making new products from used materials is recycling.

questions.q: Useful materials obtained from nature are called:
questions.explanation: Useful materials from nature are natural resources.

questions.q: Which gas in the air do we need for breathing?
questions.explanation: We breathe in oxygen from the air.

questions.q: The loose top layer of the Earth in which plants grow is:
questions.explanation: Soil is the top layer in which plants grow.

questions.q: Useful substances dug out from rocks, like iron and copper, are:
questions.explanation: Minerals are useful substances obtained from rocks.

questions.q: Resources that do not run out or are quickly replaced are:
questions.explanation: Renewable resources do not run out, like sunlight and wind.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Sunlight is renewable; it never runs out.

questions.q: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are together called:
questions.explanation: These non-renewable fuels formed from once-living things are fossil fuels.

questions.q: Fossil fuels are non-renewable because they:
options: Took millions of years to form and will run out
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels took millions of years to form, so they cannot be quickly replaced.

questions.q: Using resources wisely so enough is left for the future is called:
questions.explanation: Wise use that protects the future is sustainability.

questions.q: The three R's of resource care are:
questions.explanation: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle are the three R's.

questions.q: Switching off lights and fans when not in use is an example of:
questions.explanation: Using less and not wasting is 'Reduce'.

questions.q: Sending used materials to be made into new products is:
questions.explanation: Making new things from used materials is recycling.

questions.q: Which is the cleaner, renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation: Solar energy is renewable and does not pollute.

questions.q: Planting trees (afforestation) helps by:
options: Protecting soil, giving oxygen and supporting wildlife
questions.explanation: Trees protect soil, give oxygen and support wildlife.

questions.q: Most of the Earth's water is:
questions.explanation: Most of Earth's water is salty sea water; only a little is usable fresh water.

questions.q: A forest is usually called a renewable resource, but it can become non-renewable if it is:
options: Cut down faster than new trees can grow
questions.explanation: If trees are removed faster than they regrow, even a forest can be used up.

questions.q: Why does using solar and wind power help reduce air pollution?
options: They make electricity without burning fuels
questions.explanation: Sun and wind generate power without burning fuels, so they cause little pollution.

questions.q: A family carries cloth bags, uses both sides of paper and refills bottles. They are mainly practising:
questions.explanation: Using things again instead of throwing them away is reuse.

questions.q: Only a small part of Earth's water can be used by us because most of it is:
questions.explanation: Most water is salty sea water or frozen in ice, leaving little usable fresh water.

questions.q: Soil is treated as a precious resource partly because it:
options: Takes a very long time to form
Can be made in a factory quickly
questions.explanation: Soil forms extremely slowly over a long time, so it must be protected.

questions.q: The best overall reason to follow the three R's is to:
options: Make resources last longer and reduce waste and pollution
questions.explanation: Reduce, Reuse and Recycle conserve resources and cut waste and pollution.
